entries.title: JADE
entries.body:
*Hardware wallet* made by Blockstream, designed to secure Bitcoin private keys and compatible with the Liquid network. The Jade stands out for its original security model: instead of using a *secure element* chip, it relies on a "*virtual secure element*" model in which the private key is encrypted and can only be decrypted by combining a secret stored on the device with a secret held by the Blockstream server (or a personal server).

Jade firmwares are fully open source. The devices have a camera for *air-gapped* mode via QR codes, and work with Blockstream Green, Sparrow Wallet or other compatible software. There are 2 hardware wallets in the Jade family: the classic Blockstream Jade, available pre-assembled or as a DIY kit, and the Blockstream Jade Plus, the most recent and more premium model, featuring a large color screen and a polished UX.

entries.title: JAM
entries.body: JAM is a web interface for JoinMarket focused on ease of use. JoinMarket is a coinjoin implementation on Bitcoin, but using it from the command line can intimidate beginner users. JAM was created precisely to make JoinMarket's advanced features accessible to beginners.

entries.title: JAN3
entries.body: Company founded in 2022 by Samson Mow, former chief strategy officer of Blockstream. The name "JAN3" refers to January 3, 2009, the date on which Satoshi Nakamoto created Bitcoin's genesis block. Jan3 is dedicated to accelerating Bitcoin adoption at the nation-state level, by developing infrastructure based on layers such as the Lightning Network and sidechains such as the Liquid network. The company works in particular with El Salvador and the autonomous region of Madeira to integrate Bitcoin into their financial systems. Jan3 is also active in software development, notably with the Aqua wallet.

entries.title: JBOK
entries.body: JBOK wallets, an acronym for "*Just a Bunch Of Keys*" (in French "juste un trousseau de clés"), refer to old Bitcoin wallets that stored a set of independently and pseudo-randomly generated key pairs. Unlike modern HD wallets, which generate keys deterministically and hierarchically from a single seed, JBOK wallets had no hierarchical or deterministic relationship between keys. They were all independent of one another. Because of their less efficient management and the difficulty of backing them up, these wallets became obsolete and were spontaneously replaced by more advanced HD solutions, as standardized in BIP-0032.

entries.title: JIT CHANNEL
entries.body:
Lightning channel opened on the fly by a Lightning service provider (LSP) at the moment an incoming payment arrives for a client that does not yet have a channel. The term "JIT" (*just-in-time*) means that the channel is created only at the precise moment it is needed, and not in advance.

The mechanism relies on the LSPS2 protocol (bLIP-0052). The client asks the LSP for the opening fee parameters, then obtains a temporary SCID that it includes in its Lightning invoice as a routing hint. When a payer sends the payment, the LSP intercepts the HTLC, opens a zero-confirmation channel to the client and forwards the payment, deducting the opening fee from the amount received. The client claims the payment by revealing the preimage.

Two trust models exist:
* in the default model, the LSP broadcasts the funding transaction before receiving the preimage, which leaves the client the possibility of verifying its validity;
* in the alternative model, the client transmits the preimage immediately after the HTLC is committed.

This mechanism should not be confused with *JIT routing*, which consists of rebalancing existing channels.

entries.title: JIT ROUTING
entries.body:
Technique proposed by René Pickhardt in 2019 that allows a Lightning routing node to rebalance its channels on the fly in order to forward a payment that would otherwise have been rejected for lack of sufficient liquidity on the outgoing channel. The term "JIT" (*just-in-time*) indicates that the rebalancing is triggered at the precise moment the incoming HTLC arrives, and not preventively.

Concretely, when an intermediate node receives an HTLC to forward but lacks funds on the outgoing channel, it briefly suspends the relay and performs a circular payment through its other channels to move the necessary liquidity. The node exploits its local knowledge of the network to quickly compute low-cost rebalancing cycles. If the rebalancing succeeds and the fees incurred are lower than the routing fees collected, the operation is profitable.

*JIT routing* requires no protocol change: it is a local behavior that each routing node can adopt independently.

This mechanism should not be confused with *JIT channels*, which refer to the on-the-fly opening of a channel by an LSP.

entries.title: JOININBOX
entries.body: Minimalist Linux environment designed for using JoinMarket. JoininBox has a terminal-based menu, and provides all the basic JoinMarket commands. It makes it possible to use the JoinMarket coinjoin implementation on a machine dedicated to this task, such as a Raspberry Pi for example.

entries.title: JOINMARKET
entries.body: Coinjoin implementation created in 2015 by Chris Belcher. JoinMarket stands out from other coinjoin implementations through its unique model for matching users. It works as a P2P marketplace where "*makers*" make their bitcoins available for mixing and receive fees, while "*takers*" use this liquidity, in exchange for payment, to carry out coinjoins with them.

entries.title: JOINPOOL
entries.body:
Type of layer-2 payment system based on the shared ownership of one or more UTXOs, without the need for trust. When funds are withdrawn from a pool in this type of system, it must be impossible to determine on-chain which user made the spend.

The fundamental principle of a joinpool-type system is therefore UTXO sharing to improve Bitcoin's scalability: rather than each participant owning one or more individual UTXOs, a single UTXO represents the funds of the entire group. Each member retains the ability to unilaterally withdraw their funds at any time, either via pre-signed transactions, or through mechanisms proposed at the protocol level such as covenants. Without covenants, the interactivity required between participants increases significantly, because any change to the state of the pool requires the signature of all members.

The Ark protocol can be considered a concrete implementation of the joinpool concept, where an *Ark Service Provider* acts as coordinator and liquidity provider for the participants of the pool.

This type of system is sometimes also referred to as a "*coinpool*" or "*payment pool*".

entries.title: JOINSTR
entries.body: Decentralized coinjoin protocol that uses Nostr as a communication layer. Proposed in August 2022 by the pseudonymous developer "1440000bytes", it eliminates the need for a central coordinator, which traditionally constitutes a point of failure in coinjoin implementations. Participants register their outputs via Nostr relays, then the system creates a partially signed Bitcoin transaction (PSBT) that each participant signs individually. Once all signatures have been collected, the combined transaction is broadcast on the network.
